text: I think about how does a yoga studio actually function. It's obviously just a room with mats, very quiet, calm. But there's so much more to it than just mats. It is a business, it is a community, it is a scheduling. So first of all, if you come into a yoga studio, you will first encounter the front desk. And the front desk has a very important role. First, to welcome people, to check in people. And some studios will ask for waivers to be signed before you do class, that type of thing. They will tell you where to put your shoes, where to put your bag, where to put your coat. Sometimes, for people that are new to yoga, they will give them a little orientation and say, hey, this is where the props are, this is how you set up your mat, and this is what to expect. And they will also sell class passes, they will sell memberships, they will sell reservations, they will collect payment. So a lot of studios, their front desk is really the social hub of their business. People come in and ask questions, people recognize each other. Second thing is scheduling. Most studios offer different types of classes, hatha yoga, vinyasa, yin, restorative, power, hot yoga, etc. And they usually label them with levels, so beginner, intermediate, advanced, etc. And they will schedule them accordingly. So we will see early morning classes for people that have work, mid-day classes for people that have more flexible schedule. We will see evening classes for people that come after work. We will see weekend workshops, teacher trainings, things like that. So a studio needs to figure out what classes are filling up and what classes are not, and then adjust their schedule accordingly. And also the capacity of the room, the availability of the teachers, the season, all of that matters. Third thing is teachers. Teachers are very important for the practice, of course. Teachers are not just leading you through a pose. Teachers are assessing the room, they are assessing the students, they are creating a sequence that is safe, that is dynamic, that will challenge people and also slow them down. They will give you alternatives, they will demonstrate alternatives. They will ask you if you're hurting, what you're feeling. And they will create a safe space, a calm space where you can concentrate and focus. They come early, they prepare the room, they come early, they set up the music, they set up the lights, they stay later to answer questions. Most teachers are freelancers, independent contractors, they are paid per class, or they are paid by headcount, or they are paid flat rate. And most of them will be teaching at several studios in order to fill their hours. Fourth thing is the business model. So studios will make money from drop-ins, they will make money from passes, they will make money from memberships, from workshops, from retail, from teacher trainings, things like that. Their expenses are rent, it's utilities, it's insurance, it's cleaning, it's props, booking system, marketing, paying teachers, etc. And because rent does not change whether you have an empty class or a full class, they really need to attract regular people, regular members, so they can have a very predictable income. And so that's why they will try to convert people from drop-ins to memberships. They will offer a first class or a first few classes for very cheap and then try to convert them into regulars. And some studios are for-profit, some are non-profit, some are co-ops, some are community spaces. And some will have a sliding scale or a pay what you can model, etc. Fifth thing is the space itself, the operations. So the floor has to be cleaned, the room has to be cleaned, the temperature and the humidity has to be managed. The props have to be cleaned, have to be replaced sometimes. The sound system, the lights, the mirrors, the ventilation, all of that is important. And then there's a lot of behind the scenes. So you have the booking system, the waitlist, the cancellation, the refund, the communication with students, the marketing, the social media, the email newsletter, the community events, things like that. And some studios, like a hot yoga studio, will really have to focus on the ventilation and heating. Other studios, that are very quiet and restorative, they will focus more on the lighting, etc. And then the last thing is community. So a yoga studio, when it's functioning well, is very much a community. People will be friends, teachers will know people's names, they will know their injuries, they will know their goals. They will host workshops, retreats, charity classes, meditation sessions. So it's really a space where you can relax and calm down and really feel welcome. And that will help with retention. People don't come to the studio just to do exercise, they come to feel community, to feel belonging. But at the same time, the studio has to keep a certain level of professionalism and boundaries in order to create an inclusive space that does not become cliquey, that is welcoming for everybody, that has safety and ethics. So that's a little bit about how a yoga studio works.
